help.intro: A short text of about 150 words about the most important night in recent German history: 9 November 1989, when the Berlin Wall opened after 28 years. The text tells you what the Wall was, how long it was, why it was built, what happened on that evening and what you can still see of it today. All facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: war and hatte for the past (Die Mauer war 155 Kilometer lang. Berlin hatte zwei Teile.) and your first Perfekt forms (Die Menschen haben gefeiert. Sie sind über die Grenze gegangen). Read for the gist first, then find one number, one date or one event per question.
help.tips[0].title: war and hatte: the past of sein and haben
help.tips[0].text: sein → war: ich war, du warst, er/sie war, wir waren, sie waren. haben → hatte: ich hatte, du hattest, er/sie hatte, wir hatten, sie hatten. These two are the first past forms you need; everything else at this level uses the Perfekt. Die Mauer war 155 Kilometer lang. Berlin hatte zwei Teile. Die Menschen waren glücklich.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: The Wall was there for 28 years. Berlin had a border in the middle.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: In the evening thousands of people were at the border. They had no fear any more.
help.tips[0].check.why: wir takes waren; war is ich/er; hatten would mean 'had'.
help.tips[1].title: Perfekt: haben or sein + ge-…
help.tips[1].text: The Perfekt tells what happened: haben/sein in position 2, the participle at the end. Most verbs take haben: Die Menschen haben gefeiert, getanzt, gesungen. Verbs of movement take sein: Sie sind gegangen, gefahren, gekommen. Regular participles: ge- + stem + -t (gefeiert, getanzt, geöffnet). Irregular ones you learn as words: gegangen, gekommen, gesungen, gefallen.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: On 9 November 1989 the border soldiers opened the gates.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: Thousands went to West Berlin that night.
help.tips[1].check.q: Die Menschen ____ auf der Mauer getanzt.
help.tips[1].check.why: tanzen is not a verb of movement from A to B; it takes haben: haben getanzt.
help.remember[0]: war / waren, hatte / hatten: the past of sein and haben.
help.remember[1]: Perfekt: haben + gefeiert, geöffnet; sein + gegangen, gekommen (movement).
help.exam: Short texts about a historical event with dates, numbers and multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: For 28 years a wall ran through a city. Then, one evening in November, it opened. Read what happened in that night.
passageTranslation:
From 1961 to 1989 Berlin was a city with two parts: West Berlin and East Berlin. In the middle was the Wall. It was 155 kilometres long and almost four metres high. The government of East Germany built the Wall in August 1961. The people in the East were not allowed into the West.

Families suddenly had a border in the middle. A grandmother lived in the East, her grandchildren in the West. For 28 years it was like that.

In autumn 1989 many people in the East were on the streets. They demonstrated and shouted: 'We are the people!' On the evening of 9 November 1989 a politician said on television: the border is open. Thousands of people went straight to the Wall. At 11 pm the soldiers opened the gates. People laughed, cried, danced and sat on the Wall. It was a big party.

A year later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was one country again. Today you see the Wall only in a few places. One part stands by the Spree: the East Side Gallery, 1.3 kilometres long, with many pictures.
questions[0].explanation: "Sie war 155 Kilometer lang und fast vier Meter hoch." 1.3 km is the East Side Gallery today.
questions[1].explanation: "Die Regierung von Ost-Deutschland hat die Mauer im August 1961 gebaut."
questions[1].questionTranslation: When did East Germany build the Wall?
questions[2].explanation: hatten = past of haben for wir/sie (Familien). The past of sein would be waren.
questions[2].questionTranslation: 'Families suddenly had a border in the middle.' Which form is hatten?
questions[2].optionsTranslation[0]: present of haben for wir and sie, like wir haben
questions[3].explanation: "28 Jahre lang war das so." 1961 to 1989.
questions[3].questionTranslation: How long was the Wall there?
questions[4].explanation: "Sie haben demonstriert und gerufen: ‚Wir sind das Volk!‘"
questions[4].questionTranslation: What did the people shout in autumn 1989?
questions[5].explanation: "Um 23 Uhr haben die Soldaten die Tore geöffnet." The politician spoke earlier that evening.
questions[5].questionTranslation: What happened on 9 November 1989 at 11 pm?
questions[6].explanation: Verbs of movement from one place to another (gehen, kommen, fahren) take sein in the Perfekt.
questions[6].questionTranslation: 'Thousands of people went straight to the Wall.' Why sind and not haben?
questions[6].optionsTranslation[1]: because Menschen is plural and the plural always takes sein
questions[7].explanation: "Ein Teil steht an der Spree: die East Side Gallery, 1,3 Kilometer lang, mit vielen Bildern."
questions[7].questionTranslation: What is the East Side Gallery?
questions[7].optionsTranslation[0]: a big museum in West Berlin with pictures of the Wall
questions[7].optionsTranslation[1]: a part of the Wall by the Spree with many pictures
